title: Maker of heaven and earth
hookLine: the world is made, meant and good (Genesis 1:31)

cards: A meal. A birthday card. A shelf that's only slightly crooked.
A garden bed. Making something by hand often ends with a small moment: the maker steps back and looks. A breath out.
That's good. Not perfect, maybe, but good, and theirs, and meant. The creed's very first sentence says that about everything.

After I believe in God the Father Almighty comes: Maker of heaven and earth. And the Bible's first chapter ends with God stepping back to look at all of it: light and sea, trees and fish, animals and people.

teach.b: The Bible opens: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The Hebrew verb for created is bara, and here's the surprise: when it means create, in the Bible, its subject is always God.
People make, build, shape. Only God bara. Christians draw three things from this line.
First, the world is made. It isn't an accident, and it isn't God. It's distinct from God, the way a song is distinct from the singer.
Christian thinkers from the second century on said God made it out of nothing, not from material already lying around.
Second, the world is meant. It has a purpose. It's here because someone wanted it to be.
Third, the world is good. Six times in Genesis 1, God sees that what was made is good.
The seventh time, looking at everything together, people included: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." That mattered in the early church.

teach.h: GOOD: THE BODY IS NO PRISON.
teach.b: Some teachers, often called Gnostics, taught that the material world was a mistake or a prison, and the body something to escape. The church said no. Matter, bodies, food, sex, earth, stars: made by God, and good.
Christians today read Genesis in different ways alongside science. Some read the six days as literal days.
Many churches, Catholic and many Protestant, see no conflict between creation and evolution: Genesis tells who and why, science tells how. They differ on how, but share the same first line. Made.

how: Christians say "Maker of heaven and earth" in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds, give thanks for creation in grace before meals, and many churches keep a Season of Creation each autumn.

to create, with only God as the one creating
to bless something and call it good

games.q: what's inside the line — tap the pairs.
p: to create: only God does it

games.q: it's the second century. a teacher tells your church that the body is a prison and the physical world is a mistake. what does the church say?
o: no: matter and bodies are made by God and good.
games.why: the church rejected it, pointing to Genesis: "behold, it was very good."

practice: Look at something near you, a leaf, your own hand, a cup, the sky out the window, the way you'd look at something you'd made yourself: its color, its shape, how it works. Then quietly say: very good.
If you pray, thank God, Maker of heaven and earth, for it; if you don't, just let yourself see it as good, and meant.

wordCard.voice: Bara. The Hebrew verb for create, used in the Bible only with God as its subject: the world made, meant, and very good.

orig.note: Hebrew: he created. In this sense, the Bible gives it only God as subject.

carryVoice: Your line: very good. The seventh look, at everything together. Day two hundred ninety-eight, done.
